feedback: If the child says 'red is certain', take out and show a blue counter (pick one deliberately, or keep drawing until one comes out, since a single random draw is usually red): 'Certain? But look, here is a blue I could pull. So is red certain, or only likely?' — let the over-strong word fail against a real possible outcome.

If the child says 'even chance' because there are two colours, count together: '7 red vs 3 blue is not equal, so it is not an even chance — what would the bag need for red and blue to be an even chance?' (equal numbers).
If the child accepts '7 on a 1–6 die is very unlikely', ask 'could it EVER come up? Which faces are on the die?' — since there is no 7, it cannot happen, so it is impossible, not merely rare.
If the child calls a green draw 'very unlikely', ask 'could it EVER happen? Show me a green counter.' There is none, so it is impossible, not merely rare.
If the child treats blue (unlikely) as 'impossible', point out some blue counters are present, so it can still happen — contrast 'rarely' with 'never'.
Affirm reasons grounded in counts ('most are red, so likely') and press on reasons grounded in desire ('I want red') by asking what the counters show.
activities.intendedInsight: Each likelihood word corresponds to how many of each outcome there are; 'likely' is not a guarantee and 'impossible' (cannot happen at all) is stronger than 'very unlikely' (rare but possible). 'Even chance' requires equal numbers, not merely two possible outcomes.
learnerActions: Look into a bag you can see holds mostly red counters (e.g. 7 red and 3 blue) with the composition visible.
Before any draw, say in words how likely a red draw is and WHY, grounding the reason in the numbers ('most of them are red') rather than wanting red.

When you declare red 'certain', watch the game-master take out and show a blue counter (picked on purpose, or by drawing until one appears, because a single random draw will usually be red), then repair your word: was red certain, or only likely? Explain the difference.

Answer the opposite trap: the game-master suggests 'landing on 7 with this ordinary 1–6 die is only very unlikely, isn't it?' — decide whether 7 is very unlikely (rare but possible) or impossible (cannot happen at all), and say why.
Describe a green draw ('there are no green counters'), and a 'red or blue' draw ('only those two colours exist'), choosing and justifying a word for each.
Reject vague answers: if you say '50-50', be ready for 'but there are 7 red and 3 blue — is that even?' and recount to decide.
activities.title: The Chance-master's bag: say it, then watch it happen

feedback: If every event lands at the extremes or at 'even chance', ask for a reason tied to counts or frequency, and nudge toward the graded middle only for events that are not truly all-or-none or equally balanced.
If an unequal spinner/bag is called 'even chance', compare the total size or count for the outcome against the total for everything else: if those two totals are unequal, it cannot be an even chance.
Praise placements justified by 'most/few/none' rather than by what the child hopes happens.
activities.intendedInsight: Events can be ordered along a graded scale from impossible to certain, and placement is decided by composition, not by preference — unequal situations sit away from 'even chance'.
learnerActions: Set up a washing line or paper strip labelled impossible → unlikely → even chance → likely → certain.

Peg everyday, personally-meaningful events onto it, saying your placement aloud: 'it will get dark tonight', 'it will snow in July', 'I'll flip heads', 'the sun will rise tomorrow' (for the weather and daylight events, think about where you live: snow in July is likely in some southern places, and near the poles there are times with no sunset or no sunrise).
Move to structured chance devices where composition is inspectable — bags of counters, spinners with equal and unequal sections — and peg outcomes from those.
Place at least one deliberately unequal situation (7 red/3 blue; a spinner with one big section) and justify why it is NOT an even chance.
Say out loud the reason for each placement, referring to how many of each outcome there are.
activities.title: Physical likelihood line: peg real events and justify
